presentingComplaint: Two large-volume vomits of fresh blood and black tarry stools with collapse at home
history: Known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, prior grade II oesophageal varices banded 8 months ago, non-adherent to carvedilol) presents after two episodes of massive haematemesis (approx 500 mL fresh blood each) over 3 hours followed by three episodes of melaena and a witnessed syncopal collapse while walking to the toilet. He reports light-headedness, cold clammy peripheries and increasing drowsiness during transfer. No fever, no cough, no dysuria, no abdominal pain of note. Last drink 2 days ago. On no anticoagulants. The overlapping picture (jaundice, ascites, mild confusion) initially raised concern for decompensation/sepsis, but the dominant, time-critical problem is acute blood loss with haemodynamic collapse.
examination: Cold, mottled peripheries with prolonged capillary refill (>4 s), thready pulse. Pallor of conjunctivae. Drowsy but rousable, GCS 14 (E3V5M6), grade 1 asterixis. Stigmata of chronic liver disease: spider naevi, palmar erythema, mild scleral icterus, shifting dullness consistent with moderate ascites. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no guarding or Murphy sign. PR examination reveals melaena. No focal neurology, no meningism. Chest clear.
imaging: Bedside FAST: moderate ascites, no free intraperitoneal air/haemorrhage. Erect CXR normal, no free air under diaphragm. Urgent upper GI endoscopy after resuscitation: large oesophageal varices with active spurting (Forrest-equivalent active) bleeding, controlled by endoscopic band ligation.
microbiology: Not indicated for the shock diagnosis. Blood cultures and ascitic diagnostic tap sent given cirrhosis (SBP screen / prophylaxis decision), pending.
differentialDiagnoses: Haemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock from oesophageal variceal bleeding
finalDiagnosis: Hypovolemic (haemorrhagic) shock secondary to acute variceal haemorrhage in decompensated cirrhosis
citations: Baveno VII Consensus - Management of acute variceal haemorrhage and portal hypertension - 2022
AASLD Practice Guidance - Portal hypertensive bleeding in cirrhosis - 2016
ATLS (American College of Surgeons) - Classification and management of haemorrhagic shock - 2018
stewardship: Non-infective shock: the primary intervention is haemostatic resuscitation and source control, not antimicrobials. However, in cirrhosis with acute GI bleeding, short-course antibiotic PROPHYLAXIS (e.g., IV ceftriaxone) is guideline-mandated to reduce infection/rebleeding/mortality - this is prophylaxis, not treatment of an infection, so no empiric therapeutic antibiotic tier applies to the shock itself. Resuscitation priorities: restrictive transfusion (target Hb 7-8 g/dL), correct coagulopathy judiciously, IV terlipressin/octreotide, urgent endoscopic band ligation, consider TIPS if refractory.
contraindications: Avoid over-transfusion / aggressive volume expansion to normal BP - raises portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding (target Hb 7-8 g/dL, permissive hypotension SBP ~90-100)
Avoid indiscriminate FFP/platelet correction to normal values in cirrhosis (rebalanced haemostasis; volume overload risk)
Avoid non-selective NSAIDs and nephrotoxins given renal impairment / hepatorenal risk
edgeCases: Urea disproportionately high relative to creatinine reflects an upper GI blood 'protein meal' plus prerenal state, not primarily renal disease
Coexisting cirrhosis can mask tachycardia if on beta-blockade and lower baseline BP, causing under-estimation of shock severity
Confusion may be dual: hypoperfusion AND precipitated hepatic encephalopathy from the GI blood load
expectedMaiK: Recognise haemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock from variceal bleeding as the immediate life threat; resuscitate with blood products using a restrictive strategy, give vasoactive therapy (terlipressin) plus antibiotic prophylaxis, and secure source control by urgent endoscopy - do not anchor on decompensated cirrhosis or sepsis.
